cartas.titulo: GMO Quarterly Letter 4Q 2025 — It's Probably a Bubble, But There Is Plenty Else to Invest In (Ben Inker)
cartas.tesis_gestora: The letter articulates an 'agnostic investor's playbook' from GMO's Asset Allocation team (Ben Inker). The core thesis: AI looks like a classic investment bubble with very high valuations and rampant speculation, but a bubble-agnostic investor — one who recognizes the evidence but isn't fully convinced — can today build a portfolio that strongly outperforms if the bubble bursts and also does just fine if all assets are fairly priced. Crucially, the 2025 AI Bubble resembles the 2000 Internet Bubble (not the 2007-8 Everything Bubble nor the 2021 Duration Bubble): tilting away from AI/U.S. large caps toward non-U.S. equities, deep value stocks, and liquid alternatives 'may save investors a lot of pain if it turns out we are in a bubble without meaningfully reducing expected returns if financial markets are somehow still fairly priced today'. The framework is valuation-driven dynamic asset allocation that assumes mean reversion over 7-10 years — no need to time the bubble's burst.
cartas.decisiones_tomadas: GMO's Benchmark-Free Allocation Strategy current positioning (Q4 2025): ~50% equities (zero/minimal U.S. large cap; instead U.S. Opportunistic Value 5%, Resource Equity 4%, Developed ex-U.S. 6%, Int'l Opportunistic Value 9%, Japan Fundamental Value 6%, Japan Small Value 3%, Dev ex-U.S. Small Cap Value 5%, Emerging Markets 10%), Equity Dislocation 15% (18.9% total inclusive of Alt Allocation), Alternative Allocation 13%, ~28% liquid alternatives total, U.S. Treasury Notes 19%, ABS/Structured Products 2%, Emerging Debt 2%. The portfolio is explicitly tilted toward deep value, Japan, and non-U.S. small value; U.S. large caps are 'most notable for their absence'.
cartas.contexto_mercado: The S&P 500 is trading at valuation levels only seen during the Internet Bubble — above the 1929 and 2021 peaks on Shiller's Total Return CAPE and at all-time highs on price/sales and price/book. Rampant speculation everywhere: Thinking Machines raised $2B at a $10B valuation 'apparently without telling investors what their plan was', then $50B three months later; AMD jumped 24% the day it announced its OpenAI deal and Oracle leapt 36% on theirs; OpenAI 'a company whose revenues would have to rise a hundredfold to make good on its promises'; Palantir trades at 120x sales but Rigetti Computing and D-Wave Quantum trade at 1007x and 318x sales respectively. AI-related stocks (Nvidia driven by genuine earnings; Tesla by 'unrelenting hopes despite rapidly diminishing cash flow') have driven the S&P 500 above its 2021 valuation peak. The September 2025 risk/reward scatterplot looks strikingly similar to June 2000: slope +0.4, U.S. large caps the most overvalued asset, equal-weighted risk portfolio offering much higher expected return than MSCI World.
cartas.outlook: Today's opportunity set is closer to a 2000-style bubble than 2007 or 2021 — meaning the agnostic investor doesn't need certainty about whether AI is a bubble to move to a portfolio less dependent on the AI trade. Value stocks everywhere are very cheap; in the U.S. and EAFE markets deep value trades at some of the widest discounts on record. Non-U.S. small value is also attractive, particularly in Japan (undervalued yen + opening market for corporate control). Liquid alternatives benefit from decent cash yields and wide valuation spreads. Government bonds are priced to provide capital gains in a recession and a decent yield if the global economy holds together. Risk: if markets keep rallying broadly, the 2000-like setup could turn into a 2007- or 2021-like dilemma — but that would require good returns from a wide array of assets, not just continued AI levitation.
citas_textuales: It is difficult to get a man to understand something, when his salary depends upon his not understanding it.
AI looks like a classic investment bubble to us, with very high valuations and signs of rampant speculation.

The 2025 AI Bubble looks little like either of those two and much more like the 2000 Internet Bubble, in which a bubble-agnostic investor could have owned a portfolio with a reasonable risk/reward trade-off in either a bubble or a business-as-usual scenario.

Tilting a portfolio away from AI names and toward those assets may save investors a lot of pain if it turns out we are in a bubble without meaningfully reducing expected returns if financial markets are somehow still fairly priced today.

Today, building a diversified portfolio of risk assets that are priced to deliver equity-like-or-better returns is straightforward. While in this portfolio U.S. equities are most notable for their absence, there are still plenty of assets to choose from.
As bubbles go, AI looks like one of the easy ones for an agnostic investor to handle.
A rising tide need not only lift the most expensive boats.

cartas.resultado_real: GMO Benchmark-Free Allocation Strategy: +17.9% in 2025 (as of Nov 12, 2025), more than 4.5% ahead of a 60% MSCI World/40% Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond portfolio and 4.1% ahead of the S&P 500. Since end-2021 Duration Bubble peak: +20.8% net of fees vs. +6.8% for 60/40 ACWI/Agg. Forward expected return: 6.5% real if forecasts spot on, 4.5% real if all assets prove fairly priced (vs. 0.2% real for 60/40).
